questions.prompt: Which statement correctly defines the relationship between the ANSI/ISO SQL standard and a vendor's SQL dialect, such as T-SQL?
options: A vendor dialect is the standard's common core plus that vendor's own extensions and deviations — no vendor ships the standard unmodified.
The ANSI/ISO standard and a vendor dialect are two names for the exact same thing; "dialect" is just informal slang for the standard.
A vendor dialect is a strict subset of the standard, supporting only the features the standard actually defines.
The ANSI/ISO standard is Microsoft's internal name for T-SQL, used by other vendors as a licensing term.
A vendor dialect only exists for procedural code like stored procedures; plain SELECT/FROM/WHERE is always pure standard SQL with no vendor involvement.
Vendor dialects are generated automatically from the standard by a compliance tool, so no vendor design decisions are actually involved.
questions.explain: Every platform in this course implements the common core of the ANSI/ISO standard and then adds its own extensions on top, sometimes diverging from the standard outright where its own history (like T-SQL and Sybase's shared 1980s ancestor) pulled it a different direction. Basic SELECT/FROM/WHERE/ORDER BY is where the standard is strongest and the dialects agree almost completely; the divergence shows up specifically where the standard left gaps or vendors competed on features.
questions.distractorExplain: Option C gets the general shape right — a dialect is related to the standard — but inverts the relationship: a dialect is a superset of what the standard defines (the standard's core plus proprietary additions like Oracle's CONNECT BY or SQL Server's CROSS APPLY), not a stripped-down subset that only supports standard features.

questions.prompt: Match each platform to the description of its dialect, per Lesson 2.
right: Built from scratch in the 1990s, with its own distinct procedural syntax
Transact-SQL, sharing roots with Sybase from the 1980s
Known for standards compliance, with PL/pgSQL for procedural code
Pairs standard-ish SQL with its own procedural language for anything beyond a single statement
questions.explain: SQL Server's dialect is T-SQL, sharing roots with Sybase from the 1980s. Oracle pairs standard-ish SQL with PL/SQL for anything beyond a single statement. MySQL was built from scratch in the 1990s with its own procedural syntax. PostgreSQL has a reputation for standards compliance plus PL/pgSQL for procedural code.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about why SQL dialects diverge, per Chapter 1 Lesson 1.
options: Backward compatibility with decades-old design decisions, like T-SQL and Sybase's shared ancestor, keeps old divergences visible today.
Vendors add proprietary features like Oracle's CONNECT BY or SQL Server's CROSS APPLY partly for competitive differentiation.
The ANSI/ISO standard fully standardizes procedural extensions such as stored procedures and exception handling, so T-SQL, PL/SQL, and MySQL's procedural syntax are actually identical under the hood.
Basic SELECT/FROM/WHERE/ORDER BY is where dialects diverge the most, since the standard never addressed it.
The standard is deliberately incomplete on procedural code, which is exactly why this course spends its later chapters there.
questions.explain: History (shared ancestors like T-SQL/Sybase), competitive differentiation (proprietary features like CONNECT BY and CROSS APPLY), and the standard's deliberate incompleteness around procedural extensions are the three real reasons dialects diverge. The standard has never fully standardized procedural code in a way every vendor adopted, which is exactly why T-SQL, PL/SQL, and MySQL's procedural syntax look so different — the opposite of option C's claim. And basic SELECT/FROM/WHERE/ORDER BY is actually where the standard is strongest and dialects agree almost completely — the opposite of option D's claim.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: SQL Server's free, full-featured edition intended specifically for learning and development (not a crippled trial) is called ________ Edition.
questions.explain: SQL Server Developer Edition is free and full-featured, intended exactly for learning and development — not a stripped-down trial. It's the recommended first install in Lesson 3's practice-environment setup, since most readers of this course already have it.

questions.prompt: Put these platforms in the sane install order Lesson 3 recommends for setting up a multi-dialect practice environment.
items: SQL Server (you likely already have it)
Cloud warehouse trials like Snowflake, saved for when Chapter 9 is actually reached
questions.explain: Lesson 3 recommends SQL Server first (you likely already have it), then PostgreSQL as the easiest clean install, then MySQL, then Oracle XE as the heaviest installer, and saving cloud warehouse trials for later specifically because their trial clocks are often time-limited — starting one early just burns days you haven't used yet.

questions.code:
-- Oracle (12c+)
SELECT product_name, list_price
FROM products
ORDER BY list_price DESC
FETCH FIRST 5 ROWS ONLY;
questions.prompt: Per Lesson 5's five-dialect comparison of this same top-5 query, which three platforms in this course agree on using a shared LIMIT syntax, while SQL Server and Oracle each use their own distinct keyword?
options: MySQL, PostgreSQL, and Snowflake
SQL Server, MySQL, and PostgreSQL
Oracle, MySQL, and PostgreSQL
MySQL, PostgreSQL, and Oracle (all three using FETCH FIRST)
questions.explain: In Lesson 5's side-by-side query, MySQL, PostgreSQL, and Snowflake all happen to agree on LIMIT 5, while SQL Server uses its proprietary TOP (5) and Oracle uses the newer ANSI-standard FETCH FIRST 5 ROWS ONLY. Everything else in the query — SELECT, the column list, FROM, ORDER BY ... DESC — is identical across all five platforms; only the row-limiting keyword changes.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes Oracle's VARCHAR vs. VARCHAR2 string types?
options: VARCHAR2 is Oracle's real, recommended variable-length string type; plain VARCHAR exists but is reserved for potential future behavior changes and isn't recommended.
VARCHAR and VARCHAR2 are simply two spellings of the exact same type, kept only for backward compatibility, with no real difference between them.
VARCHAR2 is Oracle's large-object text type, used instead of CLOB for anything over 4000 characters.
VARCHAR is Oracle's modern Unicode-aware type, while VARCHAR2 is the older, non-Unicode type.
VARCHAR2 only exists inside PL/SQL procedural code and can't be used as a table column type.
Oracle has no VARCHAR-family type at all; CHAR is used for all string data regardless of length.
questions.explain: Oracle's own documentation reserves plain VARCHAR for potential future changes in behavior and explicitly recommends against using it. VARCHAR2 is Oracle's real, recommended variable-length string type for ordinary string columns, with CLOB reserved separately for genuinely large text that won't fit in VARCHAR2's practical limits.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B sounds plausible — both names do look like variations on the same idea — but Oracle doesn't treat them as interchangeable: it specifically reserves VARCHAR for a possible future redefinition and tells developers not to rely on it, which is exactly why every real Oracle schema you'll encounter uses VARCHAR2 instead. Treating the two as identical misses the whole point of the warning.

questions.prompt: A developer coming from SQL Server expects a separate INT type for order_id. Why does this Oracle table use NUMBER for both columns instead?
options: Oracle has a single flexible NUMBER(precision, scale) type that covers both integer-like values (scale 0) and fixed-point decimals (positive scale), unlike SQL Server's separate INT and DECIMAL types.
NUMBER(10) and NUMBER(10,2) are actually a bug in this table design; one of the two columns should have been declared VARCHAR2 instead.
Oracle does have a true INT type, but it has been fully deprecated, so modern Oracle schemas are required to avoid it entirely.
NUMBER is only valid for currency columns; order_id should have used Oracle's ROWID type instead.
questions.explain: Oracle's single, unusually flexible NUMBER type covers what SQL Server splits across INT, DECIMAL, and more. NUMBER(10) with no scale behaves like an integer, while NUMBER(10,2) behaves like a fixed-point decimal — both through the same underlying type. A developer used to a separate INT type is surprised the first time they see every numeric column in an Oracle schema declared as NUMBER.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about date/time types across SQL Server, Oracle, MySQL, and PostgreSQL, per Chapter 2 Lesson 3.
options: Oracle's DATE type always includes a time component down to the second, unlike SQL Server's genuinely date-only DATE type.
MySQL's TIMESTAMP is timezone-aware (stored in UTC and converted on retrieval) and has a narrower range than DATETIME.
PostgreSQL's TIMESTAMPTZ fills a role comparable to SQL Server's DATETIMEOFFSET — both store/handle timezone information explicitly.
MySQL's DATETIME is timezone-aware, while its TIMESTAMP is not.
SQL Server's DATETIME2 is the legacy, lower-precision timestamp type, now superseded by the modern DATETIME type.
questions.explain: Oracle's DATE always carries a time component to the second, a real quirk that surprises developers coming from SQL Server's genuinely date-only DATE. MySQL's TIMESTAMP is the timezone-aware, narrower-range type, while DATETIME has a wider range with no timezone conversion — option D has this backwards. PostgreSQL's TIMESTAMPTZ is timezone-aware and comparable to DATETIMEOFFSET. And it's SQL Server's DATETIME2 that is the modern, higher-precision type, superseding the legacy DATETIME — option E also has this backwards.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: inserting an empty string into an Oracle VARCHAR2 column and reading it back returns ________, not an empty string.
questions.explain: Oracle treats an empty string ('') as NULL when it's stored in a VARCHAR2 column — a real, long-standing, documented deviation from the ANSI standard. Every other platform in this course treats '' and NULL as genuinely distinct values.

questions.prompt: Match each platform to its actual boolean idiom, per Chapter 2 Lesson 4.
right: BOOLEAN, which is literally just an alias for TINYINT(1)
A genuine native BOOLEAN type (true, false, or NULL)
BIT (0, 1, or NULL)
CHAR(1) ('Y'/'N') or NUMBER(1) by convention — no true table-column boolean traditionally
questions.explain: SQL Server has no BOOLEAN column type at all — the idiom is BIT. Oracle traditionally has no boolean column type whatsoever for table storage; developers reach for CHAR(1) or NUMBER(1) by convention. MySQL's BOOLEAN is purely an alias for TINYINT(1), not a distinct type. PostgreSQL is the one exception with a genuine native BOOLEAN type, enforced by the type system itself.

questions.prompt: What do these two SELECT statements actually return against the row just inserted?
options: The IS NULL query matches the row; the = '' query matches nothing at all, because Oracle stores '' as NULL, and = NULL never matches anything on any platform.
The IS NULL query matches nothing; the = '' query matches the row, the same behavior as SQL Server and PostgreSQL.
Both queries match the row, since Oracle treats '' and NULL as fully interchangeable in every kind of comparison, including equality.
Both queries return an error, because VARCHAR2 columns can't store an empty string value at all.
questions.explain: Oracle stores the inserted '' as NULL, so middle_name IS NULL matches the row. But = NULL never matches anything on any of this course's platforms — that rule is universal — so middle_name = '' matches nothing at all, even though the value was originally inserted as an empty string literal.

questions.prompt: What does Oracle actually do behind the scenes to make this modern IDENTITY column work?
options: It creates and manages a SEQUENCE for you automatically — the same underlying mechanism as the traditional SEQUENCE-plus-trigger pattern, just without you writing the trigger yourself.
It silently switches the column to MySQL-style AUTO_INCREMENT, which only works because Oracle added MySQL compatibility in 12c.
IDENTITY columns don't use a sequence at all — they generate values purely from the row's physical disk address.
Nothing — GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY is accepted syntax but has no real effect, and the column must still be populated manually.
questions.explain: Modern Oracle's GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY is really a SEQUENCE under the hood, with the BEFORE INSERT trigger machinery that the traditional SEQUENCE-plus-trigger pattern required by hand now handled for you automatically. It's the same core mechanism Oracle always used for auto-incrementing keys, just with a more SQL Server-like column syntax layered on top.

questions.code:
SELECT ProductID, Name, ListPrice
FROM Products
WHERE ROWNUM <= 10
ORDER BY ListPrice DESC;
questions.prompt: A developer runs this on Oracle expecting the 10 most expensive products. What does it actually return, and why?
options: An arbitrary 10 rows, only sorted afterward by price — ROWNUM is assigned to rows as they come out of the table scan, before ORDER BY ever runs, so the filter picks some 10 rows first and only then sorts just those 10.
Exactly the 10 most expensive products, because Oracle evaluates ORDER BY before WHERE whenever ROWNUM is involved.
All rows in the table, because ROWNUM <= 10 is ignored whenever an ORDER BY clause is also present.
A syntax error, because ROWNUM can never be used inside a WHERE clause.
questions.explain: ROWNUM numbers rows as they come out of the table scan, in whatever order the optimizer happens to produce — the WHERE ROWNUM <= 10 filter runs first, and only then does ORDER BY sort those already-chosen 10 arbitrary rows. The fix is to sort inside a subquery first, then number and filter the already-sorted result in an outer query (or use Oracle 12c+'s FETCH FIRST, which sidesteps the trap entirely).

questions.code:
SELECT first_name + ' ' + last_name AS full_name
FROM employees;
questions.prompt: This T-SQL-style query runs on MySQL instead of SQL Server. What actually happens?
options: + is arithmetic addition in MySQL, not concatenation — this either errors or silently coerces the strings toward 0, producing garbage, not a concatenated name.
It works identically to SQL Server, concatenating first_name and last_name with a space between them.
MySQL automatically detects that the operands are strings and switches the meaning of + to concatenation just for this statement.
It raises a syntax error immediately, because + is not a valid operator anywhere in MySQL.
questions.explain: MySQL has no string-concatenation + at all — the operator is pure arithmetic addition. Writing first_name + ' ' + last_name either errors or silently coerces the string operands toward 0, producing garbage rather than a joined name. MySQL requires CONCAT(first_name, ' ', last_name) for this, with no native operator alternative.

questions.prompt: Match each description of a pagination approach to the actual syntax it refers to, per Chapter 3 Lesson 1.
left: SQL Server's simplest row-limiting clause (no offset/skip capability)
Oracle's pre-12c pseudo-column, numbered before ORDER BY ever runs
MySQL and PostgreSQL's native pagination clause
The ANSI-standard syntax both SQL Server 2012+ and Oracle 12c+ support
right: ROWNUM
OFFSET n ROWS FETCH NEXT n ROWS ONLY
TOP (n)
LIMIT n OFFSET n
questions.explain: TOP (n) is SQL Server's simplest clause, limiting rows with no skip/offset concept at all. ROWNUM is Oracle's pre-12c pseudo-column, assigned before ORDER BY runs, which is exactly why it traps developers trying to get the top N by price. LIMIT n OFFSET n is MySQL and PostgreSQL's shared native syntax. OFFSET n ROWS FETCH NEXT n ROWS ONLY is the modern ANSI-standard form both SQL Server 2012+ and Oracle 12c+ support.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about identifier quoting, per Chapter 3 Lesson 3.
options: SQL Server's brackets ([Order]) are T-SQL-specific and always available, with no session setting required.
SQL Server also accepts double quotes for identifiers, but only when the QUOTED_IDENTIFIER session setting is ON.
MySQL's default identifier-quoting character is the backtick, with double quotes only working if ANSI_QUOTES mode is enabled.
Oracle and PostgreSQL both use backticks as their default identifier-quoting character, the same as MySQL.
Quoting an identifier on Oracle or PostgreSQL has no effect on case sensitivity — quoted and unquoted references always behave identically.
questions.explain: Brackets are always available on SQL Server with no dependency, which is why most T-SQL code uses them. SQL Server's double-quote alternative depends on QUOTED_IDENTIFIER being ON. MySQL's default is the backtick, with ANSI_QUOTES mode needed for double quotes to work instead. Oracle and PostgreSQL actually use standard double quotes, not backticks, so option D is wrong — and quoting does change case sensitivity on both platforms (a quoted identifier becomes case-sensitive exactly as typed), so option E is also wrong.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: PostgreSQL automatically folds an unquoted identifier to ________, while Oracle folds an unquoted identifier to UPPERCASE.
questions.explain: Oracle and PostgreSQL fold unquoted identifiers in opposite directions: Oracle folds to UPPERCASE, PostgreSQL folds to lowercase. Once an identifier is quoted on either platform, case matters exactly as typed — which is why mixing a quoted reference with a table that was created unquoted is a classic source of "table not found" confusion.

questions.prompt: Both queries are intended to compute the same days-to-ship value. Why does the MySQL version drop the 'day' argument that T-SQL requires?
options: MySQL's DATEDIFF(date1, date2) takes only two dates and always computes the difference in days; T-SQL's DATEDIFF(datepart, date1, date2) takes a unit as its first argument because it can compute in units other than days.
The MySQL version is actually wrong and will raise a syntax error without an explicit unit argument.
MySQL's DATEDIFF always returns the difference in months by default, unlike T-SQL's, which defaults to days.
T-SQL's extra 'day' argument is purely cosmetic in this query — removing it would change nothing about the result.
questions.explain: MySQL's DATEDIFF(date1, date2) takes exactly two arguments and always computes in days, with no unit to specify. T-SQL's DATEDIFF(datepart, date1, date2) needs that extra datepart argument because it can compute the difference in days, months, years, or other units — MySQL's simpler two-argument form is correct MySQL syntax, not a mistake.

questions.code: SELECT 1 + 1;
questions.prompt: This statement fails to run on Oracle. What's actually wrong, and what's the fix?
options: Oracle requires a FROM clause on every SELECT; DUAL, a built-in one-row, one-column table, satisfies that requirement — SELECT 1 + 1 FROM DUAL; fixes it.
1 + 1 is invalid Oracle arithmetic syntax; it must be written as 1 PLUS 1.
A FROM-less SELECT works fine on Oracle exactly like SQL Server; the real problem here is the missing semicolon.
Oracle requires every literal expression to be wrapped in TO_NUMBER() before it can be selected.
questions.explain: Oracle's SQL grammar requires a FROM clause on every SELECT statement — there's no such thing as a SELECT with no table at all. DUAL is a real, built-in system table Oracle ships with exactly one row and one column, specifically to satisfy this rule when evaluating a one-off expression like 1 + 1, SYSDATE, or UPPER('hello').

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about comments and statement terminators, per Chapter 3 Lesson 7.
options: -- and /* */ comments behave identically across T-SQL, Oracle, MySQL, and PostgreSQL.
GO is a signal understood by SSMS and sqlcmd to split a script into batches — it is not part of the SQL language itself, and the server has no idea what it means.
Oracle, MySQL, and PostgreSQL all effectively require a semicolon to terminate a statement, especially once a script has more than one statement.
Pasting GO into Oracle's SQL*Plus or PostgreSQL's psql works fine, since GO is part of the ANSI SQL standard.
T-SQL has always strictly required a semicolon after every single statement, with no exceptions.
questions.explain: Comments are one of the rare areas with zero divergence across all four dialects. GO is purely a client-tool batch separator for SSMS/sqlcmd, understood by the tool, not the server, and not part of SQL at all — which is exactly why pasting it into Oracle's SQL*Plus or PostgreSQL's psql produces a syntax error, not option D's claim that it works. Oracle, MySQL, and PostgreSQL effectively require semicolons, while T-SQL has historically let you skip them for most single statements (though newer syntax like CTEs now requires one), contradicting option E.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the correct order for Oracle's traditional (pre-12c) way of getting the 10 most expensive products, avoiding the ROWNUM trap.
items: Write the inner query with SELECT, FROM, and ORDER BY ListPrice DESC, with no ROWNUM filter yet
Wrap that sorted query as a subquery inside an outer SELECT
Apply WHERE ROWNUM <= 10 on the outer query, numbering rows only after they are already sorted
Read back the 10 most expensive rows, correctly sorted, from the outer query's result
questions.explain: Sorting has to happen first and completely, inside an inner query with its own ORDER BY. Only once that sorted result is wrapped as a subquery can an outer query apply WHERE ROWNUM <= 10 against already-sorted rows, instead of ROWNUM numbering rows before they're sorted — which is exactly the trap of filtering on ROWNUM in the same query as ORDER BY.

questions.code:
-- Oracle, attempting a full outer join with legacy syntax
SELECT o.order_id, c.customer_name
FROM orders o, customers c
WHERE o.customer_id(+) = c.customer_id(+);
questions.prompt: A developer tries to write a full outer join using Oracle's legacy (+) operator, shown above. What actually happens when this runs?
options: Oracle raises ORA-01468, because (+) cannot be placed on both sides of the same join condition
It runs fine and returns a full outer join, exactly as intended
It silently runs as an inner join, ignoring both (+) markers
It runs as a left join, using only the first (+) it encounters
questions.explain: (+) cannot express a full outer join directly — placing (+) on both sides of the same comparison raises ORA-01468. Oracle's modern FULL OUTER JOIN ... ON syntax handles this directly with no workaround needed, which is exactly one of the two concrete reasons ANSI join syntax replaced (+) everywhere, including on Oracle itself.

questions.code:
-- T-SQL — this does NOT work as the developer intended
SELECT c.CustomerName, o.OrderID
FROM Customers AS c
JOIN (
  SELECT TOP 3 OrderID, OrderDate
  FROM Orders
  WHERE Orders.CustomerID = c.CustomerID
  ORDER BY OrderDate DESC
) AS o ON 1 = 1;
questions.prompt: This query fails. What's actually wrong, and which T-SQL keyword fixes it without restructuring the query's logic?
options: A plain JOIN's right-hand subquery can't see c.CustomerID from the outer table; replacing JOIN with CROSS APPLY makes the derived table correlated
TOP 3 can never be used inside a derived table; it must be rewritten with ROW_NUMBER() instead
The ON 1 = 1 clause is invalid syntax and must be removed entirely
CustomerID must be explicitly aliased as c.CustomerID inside the subquery's own SELECT list before it becomes visible
questions.explain: A plain JOIN's right-hand subquery is evaluated independently and can't see columns from an earlier table in the same FROM clause — that's why WHERE Orders.CustomerID = c.CustomerID fails inside the derived table. CROSS APPLY lets the derived table reference c.CustomerID because it allows the right-hand side to be correlated to everything that precedes it in FROM, which is exactly the problem CROSS APPLY (and LATERAL on other platforms) exists to solve.

questions.code:
-- Copied as-is from a T-SQL recursive CTE, run unchanged on PostgreSQL
WITH EmployeeHierarchy AS (
  SELECT employee_id, manager_id, 0 AS level
  FROM employees
  WHERE manager_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.employee_id, e.manager_id, eh.level + 1
  FROM employees e
  JOIN EmployeeHierarchy eh ON e.manager_id = eh.employee_id
)
SELECT * FROM EmployeeHierarchy;
questions.prompt: A developer copies this T-SQL recursive CTE unchanged into PostgreSQL. What happens, and why?
options: It fails, because PostgreSQL requires the RECURSIVE keyword (WITH RECURSIVE) before a CTE that references itself
It runs fine, because WITH CTEs behave identically on every platform in this course regardless of recursion
It fails, because PostgreSQL has no CTE support at all
It runs, but silently returns only the anchor member's rows, never recursing
questions.explain: MySQL 8.0+ and PostgreSQL both require the RECURSIVE keyword (WITH RECURSIVE) before any CTE that references itself in its recursive member — leave it out and the self-reference to EmployeeHierarchy inside the recursive member fails to parse. T-SQL and Oracle never require, or even have, an equivalent keyword; the recursive structure alone is enough for those two engines to recognize it.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: three of the four dialects in this course — T-SQL, PostgreSQL, and MySQL 8.0.31+ — call the 'rows in the first query but not the second' set operation EXCEPT. Oracle alone calls the identical operation ________.
questions.explain: T-SQL, PostgreSQL, and MySQL 8.0.31+ all converged on the ANSI-standard name EXCEPT for this operation. Oracle alone kept its original name, MINUS — same semantics (rows in the first query that don't appear in the second), just a different keyword. Writing EXCEPT against Oracle raises a syntax error, since Oracle has never adopted that keyword.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about window functions (ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK, LAG, LEAD) across T-SQL, Oracle, MySQL 8.0+, and PostgreSQL, per Chapter 4.
options: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, and DENSE_RANK use identical OVER/PARTITION BY/ORDER BY syntax on all four platforms
Window functions were standardized in SQL:2003, and vendors implemented that standard closely
Using SUM as a window function with OVER() collapses rows into groups the same way GROUP BY does
The default frame used when no explicit ROWS/RANGE BETWEEN clause is given can differ subtly between platforms in tie situations
Named windows (WINDOW w AS (...)) are supported identically across all four platforms, including T-SQL
questions.explain: Window functions were standardized in SQL:2003, and ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK, LAG, and LEAD all use identical OVER/PARTITION BY/ORDER BY syntax across T-SQL, Oracle, MySQL 8.0+, and PostgreSQL — none of that transfers with any syntax changes. A window function never collapses rows into groups the way GROUP BY does; every original row still appears in the output, which is the whole point of OVER(). The two genuinely real, if minor, platform differences are default frame behavior in tie situations and advanced frame-clause extensions like named windows, which T-SQL doesn't support.

questions.prompt: Match each Chapter 4 term to what it actually is.
right: Required by MySQL 8.0+ and PostgreSQL before WITH, only for a CTE that references itself
Oracle's name for the set operation that returns rows in the first query not in the second
Oracle's legacy WHERE-clause outer-join marker, unable to express a full outer join directly
T-SQL's and PostgreSQL/MySQL's keywords for a derived table that can reference columns from an earlier table in the same FROM clause
questions.explain: The (+) operator is Oracle's legacy WHERE-clause outer-join marker that can't express a full outer join directly. CROSS APPLY (T-SQL) and LATERAL (PostgreSQL, MySQL 8.0.14+, and optionally Oracle) both let a derived table reference columns from an earlier table in the same FROM clause. RECURSIVE is required by MySQL 8.0+ and PostgreSQL only for a self-referencing CTE, never by T-SQL or Oracle. MINUS is simply Oracle's name for what the other three dialects call EXCEPT.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes FOR loop support across the four dialects compared in Chapter 5?
options: T-SQL has no native FOR loop at all; repeating N times requires WHILE plus a manually incremented counter, while PL/SQL and PL/pgSQL both have a genuine FOR i IN 1..10 LOOP construct
T-SQL has a native FOR loop identical to PL/SQL's FOR i IN 1..10 LOOP
None of the four dialects in this course have a native counting FOR loop
MySQL has a native FOR i IN range loop that T-SQL lacks
T-SQL's WHILE loop checks its condition after the loop body runs, the same as MySQL's REPEAT...UNTIL
PL/SQL requires a manually incremented counter for its FOR loop, exactly like T-SQL's WHILE idiom
questions.explain: T-SQL has no native FOR loop at all — WHILE plus a manually incremented counter is the only option for 'repeat N times, counting.' PL/SQL and PL/pgSQL both have a genuine FOR i IN 1..10 LOOP that handles the counter automatically, with no manual increment needed. MySQL has neither a FOR i IN range loop nor T-SQL's exact idiom, but it does have its own REPEAT...UNTIL construct, which checks its condition after the body runs.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B claims T-SQL has a FOR loop identical to PL/SQL's — it doesn't. This is exactly the single biggest control-flow gap between T-SQL and the other three dialects in this comparison: T-SQL developers reach for WHILE plus a counter precisely because no FOR i IN range construct exists in T-SQL at all.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: PostgreSQL doesn't ship with one fixed procedural language — it supports multiple pluggable 'PL' languages, but the one almost everyone uses, modeled closely on Oracle's PL/SQL shape, is called ________.
questions.explain: PostgreSQL doesn't ship with one fixed procedural language — it supports multiple pluggable 'PL' languages you install and CREATE LANGUAGE as extensions (PL/pgSQL, PL/Python, PL/Perl, and others). In practice almost everyone uses PL/pgSQL, PostgreSQL's own default, which deliberately borrows its DECLARE/BEGIN/EXCEPTION/END shape from Oracle's PL/SQL.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about MySQL's two different variable mechanisms, per Chapter 5.
options: Inside a BEGIN...END block, DECLARE ... DEFAULT creates a local variable scoped to that block
A session (user-defined) variable like @price persists for the whole client session, not just one statement
A plain DECLARE'd local variable can be used outside any BEGIN...END block, the same as a T-SQL DECLARE
Session variables and block-scoped DECLARE variables are fully interchangeable — either syntax works in either context
Session variables are prefixed with @ and assigned with := or =, independent of any stored program
questions.explain: MySQL genuinely has two different kinds of variables. Inside a BEGIN...END block, DECLARE ... DEFAULT creates a local variable scoped to that block — the MySQL equivalent of T-SQL's DECLARE. Outside any block, an @-prefixed session (user-defined) variable persists for the whole client session using := or =. The two are not interchangeable: a plain DECLARE'd variable can't exist outside a routine body, and a session @variable isn't block-scoped the way a DECLARE'd one is.

questions.code:
-- A single UPDATE statement affecting 10 rows
UPDATE products SET list_price = list_price * 1.05 WHERE product_line = 'R';
questions.prompt: This single UPDATE changes 10 rows. If a products table has an AFTER UPDATE trigger built with T-SQL's inserted/deleted virtual tables, and the identical logical trigger is built on Oracle with FOR EACH ROW and :NEW/:OLD, how many times does each trigger actually fire for this one UPDATE?
options: The T-SQL trigger fires once, with all 10 old/new row pairs available together; the Oracle FOR EACH ROW trigger fires 10 separate times, once per row
Both triggers fire exactly once, since both are reacting to the same single UPDATE statement
Both triggers fire 10 times, once per affected row, since that's how triggers work on every platform
The T-SQL trigger fires 10 times; the Oracle trigger fires once, because FOR EACH ROW actually means the opposite of what it says
questions.explain: T-SQL's set-based inserted/deleted virtual tables mean a single UPDATE affecting 10 rows fires the trigger exactly once, with all 10 old/new row pairs available together in deleted/inserted. Oracle's FOR EACH ROW triggers are row-level by default: the same 10-row UPDATE fires the trigger 10 separate times, once per row, each time with a fresh :NEW/:OLD holding just that one row's columns. T-SQL thinks in sets; Oracle thinks in rows, by default.

questions.prompt: The call above omits the OUTPUT keyword at the call site. What actually happens?
options: The procedure runs without error, but @ResultPrice is never populated with the returned price — forgetting OUTPUT at the call site fails silently
SQL Server raises an error immediately, refusing to run the procedure without OUTPUT at the call site
@ResultPrice is populated correctly anyway, since OUTPUT on the parameter definition is all that's required
The procedure call is rejected at compile time with a missing-parameter error
questions.explain: To get a value back out of a T-SQL procedure, the parameter must be marked OUTPUT in both the procedure definition AND the call. Forgetting OUTPUT at the call site doesn't raise an error — the statement still runs, it just silently fails to populate the caller's variable, which is exactly the genuinely confusing T-SQL trip-up this lesson warns about.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about parameter direction in T-SQL stored procedures versus PL/SQL procedures, per Chapter 5.
options: PL/SQL gives a genuine three-way parameter direction model: IN, OUT, and IN OUT
T-SQL only has two directional states: normal (IN-like) or OUTPUT
A PL/SQL OUT parameter is write-only, while a T-SQL OUTPUT parameter can also receive an input value
T-SQL's OUTPUT keyword only needs to appear once, on the procedure definition — the call site never needs it
PL/SQL's IN parameter direction must be written explicitly in every parameter list, since there is no default
questions.explain: PL/SQL's three-way IN/OUT/IN OUT model is more explicit than T-SQL's: T-SQL only distinguishes normal (IN-like, the default) parameters from OUTPUT ones, and a T-SQL OUTPUT parameter can also receive an input value, unlike PL/SQL's properly write-only OUT. IN is PL/SQL's default direction and doesn't need to be written explicitly, the same way a normal T-SQL parameter needs no extra keyword. T-SQL's OUTPUT keyword must appear on both the definition and the call — omitting it at the call site is the real, documented trip-up.

questions.code:
DELIMITER //
CREATE PROCEDURE GetProductPrice(
  IN  p_product_id INT,
  OUT p_price DECIMAL(10,2)
)
BEGIN
  SELECT list_price INTO p_price
  FROM products
  WHERE product_id = p_product_id;
END //
DELIMITER ;
questions.prompt: Why does this MySQL procedure definition need the DELIMITER // / DELIMITER ; wrapper at all?
options: The procedure body itself contains ordinary semicolons; without temporarily redefining the statement terminator, the client would treat the body's first semicolon as the end of the whole CREATE PROCEDURE statement
DELIMITER is required syntax inside every MySQL BEGIN...END block, regardless of whether the body contains semicolons
MySQL procedures can only be created through the DELIMITER command; CREATE PROCEDURE alone is not valid MySQL syntax
DELIMITER changes the procedure's parameter direction defaults from IN to OUT
questions.explain: The DELIMITER // / DELIMITER ; wrapper temporarily redefines the statement terminator specifically because the procedure body itself contains ordinary semicolons — without that trick, the MySQL client would treat the body's first semicolon as the end of the whole CREATE PROCEDURE statement rather than part of the body.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes table-returning function support across the four dialects in this course?
options: T-SQL has table-valued functions queryable directly in a FROM clause; PostgreSQL has RETURNS TABLE/RETURNS SETOF for the same capability; PL/SQL can only simulate it with a REF CURSOR, which must be fetched explicitly rather than queried in FROM; MySQL has no table-valued function concept at all
All four dialects in this course support genuine table-valued functions queryable directly in a FROM clause
MySQL functions can return a full result set via RETURNS TABLE, the same as PostgreSQL
PL/SQL's REF CURSOR return type can be queried directly in a FROM clause exactly like a T-SQL table-valued function
Only T-SQL supports any form of table-returning function; the other three dialects are scalar-only
questions.explain: T-SQL has genuine table-valued functions queryable directly in a FROM clause. PostgreSQL's RETURNS TABLE/RETURNS SETOF gives the identical capability. PL/SQL functions can only simulate it by returning a REF CURSOR, which the caller must fetch from explicitly — it isn't directly queryable in a FROM clause the way a true TVF is. MySQL has no table-valued function concept at all; that gap has to be worked around with a stored procedure's result set or a view instead.
questions.distractorExplain: Option C claims MySQL functions support RETURNS TABLE the same as PostgreSQL — this is exactly backwards. MySQL's lack of any table-valued function concept is the one genuine, named platform limitation in this lesson; a MySQL function can only ever return a single scalar value.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a T-SQL cursor loop checks ________ to find out whether the last FETCH succeeded, while PL/SQL's explicit cursor loop checks cur%NOTFOUND for the identical purpose instead.
questions.explain: T-SQL's cursor loop checks @@FETCH_STATUS = 0 in its WHILE condition to know the last FETCH succeeded, requiring a FETCH NEXT before the loop starts and again at the bottom of the body. PL/SQL's explicit cursor instead checks EXIT WHEN cur%NOTFOUND, a per-cursor attribute rather than a single global value — different mechanism, same underlying purpose of detecting 'no more rows.'

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about error handling across T-SQL, PL/SQL, MySQL, and PostgreSQL, per Chapter 5.
options: PL/SQL's EXCEPTION section can catch specific named exceptions like NO_DATA_FOUND before falling back to a catch-all WHEN OTHERS

MySQL's handler model requires declaring a HANDLER ahead of time, tied to a condition type, separate from the code it protects — genuinely more awkward than wrapping risky code in a single TRY or EXCEPTION block
T-SQL's single CATCH block automatically distinguishes between different error types without any extra logic
PL/pgSQL's EXCEPTION WHEN syntax is close to Oracle's, including a WHEN OTHERS catch-all and SQLERRM for the error message
A MySQL CONTINUE HANDLER stops the current block entirely the instant it fires, the same as an EXIT HANDLER
questions.explain: PL/SQL's EXCEPTION section supports specific named exceptions like NO_DATA_FOUND and TOO_MANY_ROWS before a catch-all WHEN OTHERS, more granular than T-SQL's single generic CATCH block, which catches everything the same way unless you add your own conditional logic. MySQL's DECLARE ... HANDLER model really is more awkward: the handler is declared separately from the code it protects, tied to a condition type, rather than wrapping risky code in one block the way TRY or an EXCEPTION section does. PL/pgSQL's EXCEPTION WHEN syntax is close to Oracle's, including WHEN OTHERS and SQLERRM. A MySQL CONTINUE HANDLER resumes execution after the triggering statement rather than stopping the block — that's the EXIT HANDLER's job, not CONTINUE's.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of MySQL's dynamic SQL cycle in the correct order.
items: PREPARE stmt FROM 'SELECT list_price FROM products WHERE product_id = ?';
questions.explain: MySQL's dynamic SQL cycle is three separate statements, not one: first set the bind value, then PREPARE stmt FROM the SQL text with ? placeholders, then EXECUTE stmt USING the bound variable(s), and finally DEALLOCATE PREPARE stmt to release it. This is structurally different from PL/SQL's and PL/pgSQL's single EXECUTE IMMEDIATE/EXECUTE statement that does all of this in one call.

questions.prompt: What happens when this anonymous block runs?
options: It fails at the final DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE line, because v_inner was declared inside the nested block and no longer exists once that inner block's END; runs
It runs fine, printing 'outer value / inner value' twice, because v_inner remains visible for the rest of the outer block
It fails immediately at compile time, because PL/SQL blocks can never be nested inside BEGIN...END
It runs fine, but v_outer becomes NULL once the inner block finishes
questions.explain: A block's DECLARE section creates variables scoped only to that block. v_inner is declared inside the nested inner block, so once that inner block's END; runs, v_inner no longer exists — referencing it afterward in the outer block fails. v_outer, declared in the surrounding block, remains visible the whole time, including inside the nested block.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about PL/SQL packages, per Lesson 36.
options: A package's body can be rewritten and recompiled without forcing callers or the package specification to change, as long as the spec's signatures stay the same
A private helper procedure defined only in the package body, and never listed in the spec, cannot be called from outside the package
A package-level variable is reinitialized to its default value on every single call to any procedure in the package
T-SQL has a direct language-level equivalent of a package, just under a different keyword
A package specification declares the public interface: procedure/function signatures and any public variables, cursors, or types
questions.explain: A package body's implementation can be rewritten and recompiled without touching the spec or forcing callers to change, as long as the spec's signatures stay the same — that stable-contract-vs-changeable-implementation split is the whole point of separating spec from body. A private helper that's never listed in the spec can't be called from outside the package. A package specification declares the public interface: signatures plus any public variables, cursors, or types. A package-level variable is initialized once per session and keeps its value across many separate calls — it is not reinitialized on every call. T-SQL has no construct that maps onto a package at all.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a PL/SQL block can run DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE with no error at all, yet print nothing visible, unless the client tool has first run ________, typically once at the top of the session.
questions.explain: DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE's output is buffered, and the client tool only displays that buffered text once SET SERVEROUTPUT ON has been run — typically once at the top of the session. Skip it, and the block still runs and PUT_LINE still gets called with no error, yet nothing visible appears, which is the single most common first-timer trip-up with DBMS_OUTPUT.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes what a REF CURSOR is in PL/SQL?
options: A cursor variable that can be OPENed FOR different queries at runtime and passed around, unlike an ordinary named cursor whose query is fixed at declaration time
A named cursor whose query is fixed at declaration time, exactly like the explicit cursors used for row-by-row processing
A table-valued function that can be queried directly in a FROM clause, the same as a T-SQL TVF
A PL/SQL collection type used to hold query results in memory, similar to a Nested Table
A session variable that stores the most recent query's result set for the life of the connection
A trigger-only construct used to expose :NEW and :OLD row values
questions.explain: An ordinary explicit cursor's query is fixed the moment it's declared. A REF CURSOR is a variable instead — OPEN ... FOR associates it with a specific query at runtime, and the exact same variable can later be OPENed FOR a completely different query depending on runtime logic. This is also Oracle's mechanism for handing a result set back to a caller from a procedure's OUT parameter, since a bare SELECT inside a PL/SQL procedure has nowhere to 'go' the way it does in T-SQL.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes an ordinary explicit cursor, not a REF CURSOR — the entire point of a REF CURSOR is that it's a variable, so the same declaration can be OPENed FOR a completely different query depending on runtime logic, which a fixed named cursor can never do.

questions.prompt: Match each PL/SQL collection type (or declaration clause) to what actually distinguishes it, per Lesson 39.
right: Declares a collection type's key as a string instead of an integer, making it an associative array
Has no upper bound, and — unlike the other two collection types — can also be used as a real database column type
Indexed by integer or string, exists only in memory, with no corresponding database column type at all
Declares its maximum size up front at declaration time and can never hold more elements than that
questions.explain: A VARRAY declares its maximum size up front at declaration time and can never exceed it. A Nested Table has no upper bound and — unlike either other collection type — can also be used as a real database column type. An Associative Array is indexed by integer or string and exists only in memory, with no database column equivalent at all. Declaring a collection type with INDEX BY VARCHAR2(30) is specifically what makes it an associative array keyed by a string instead of an integer.

questions.prompt: This procedure is called from inside a larger funds-transfer transaction that later fails and rolls back. What happens to the login_audit row inserted by log_login_attempt?
options: It survives the rollback, because PRAGMA AUTONOMOUS_TRANSACTION makes this procedure's transaction fully independent of the caller's, and it already committed on its own before the caller's rollback happened
It is rolled back along with everything else, because any INSERT performed during the outer transaction is swept into that same transaction
It survives only if the outer transaction also explicitly commits before rolling back, which is contradictory and never happens
It is never actually inserted at all, since an autonomous transaction cannot run until the caller's transaction finishes
questions.explain: PRAGMA AUTONOMOUS_TRANSACTION makes a block's transaction fully independent of whatever transaction called it — it can COMMIT or ROLLBACK entirely on its own, with no effect on, or from, the caller's pending work. Because log_login_attempt already committed its own INSERT before the outer transfer_funds transaction later failed and rolled back, that login_audit row survives regardless — exactly the rollback-proof audit trail this feature exists to provide, something T-SQL's nested BEGIN TRANSACTION calls cannot do since SQL Server tracks a single nesting count and an outer ROLLBACK undoes everything.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about BULK COLLECT and FORALL, per Lesson 41.
options: SELECT ... BULK COLLECT INTO fetches an entire result set into a collection in a single context switch between the PL/SQL engine and the SQL engine
FORALL sends a whole batch of INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE statements, one per collection element, to the SQL engine as a single bulk operation
Combining BULK COLLECT and FORALL is called bulk binding, a well-documented Oracle performance recommendation for substantial row-by-row work
An ordinary cursor FOR loop that fetches and updates one row at a time has no extra overhead compared to BULK COLLECT plus FORALL
FORALL can only be used with DELETE statements, never INSERT or UPDATE
questions.explain: SELECT ... BULK COLLECT INTO fetches an entire result set into a collection in one context switch instead of one switch per row. FORALL sends a whole batch of INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE statements across a collection as a single bulk operation instead of looping statement by statement — it works with any of the three DML statement types, not just DELETE. Together this is called bulk binding, a genuinely well-documented Oracle performance practice. An ordinary row-by-row cursor loop pays real context-switch overhead on every single iteration, which is exactly the cost BULK COLLECT and FORALL exist to eliminate.

questions.prompt: Translating this T-SQL IF block into idiomatic PL/SQL, per Lesson 42's checklist, which rewrite is correct?
options: IF v_order_count = 0 THEN DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE('No orders found for this customer.'); RETURN; END IF;
IF v_order_count = 0 BEGIN DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE('No orders found for this customer.'); RETURN; END;
IF v_order_count = 0 THEN DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE('No orders found for this customer.'); RETURN; END;
IF v_order_count = 0 THEN PRINT('No orders found for this customer.'); RETURN; END IF;
questions.explain: PL/SQL's IF always needs THEN and always closes with END IF (two words), regardless of how many statements are inside the branch — there's no equivalent of T-SQL's single-statement-doesn't-need-wrapping shortcut, and no BEGIN...END substitute for END IF. PRINT becomes DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE, and RETURN works the same way in both languages, exiting the procedure immediately.

questions.prompt: Match each T-SQL construct to its idiomatic PL/SQL translation, per Lesson 42's checklist.
left: A bare SELECT that returns a result set to the caller
right: DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE (plus SET SERVEROUTPUT ON to see it)
A bare parameter name marked IN/OUT/IN OUT, usually prefixed p_
A SYS_REFCURSOR OUT parameter, OPENed FOR the query
One DECLARE (or IS) section listing every local variable before BEGIN
questions.explain: T-SQL's @param keeps its sigil throughout the procedure body; PL/SQL parameters drop it, are explicitly marked IN/OUT/IN OUT, and are conventionally p_ prefixed. T-SQL lets DECLARE appear scattered anywhere in the batch; PL/SQL requires every local variable in one DECLARE (or IS) section before BEGIN. PRINT becomes DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE (plus SET SERVEROUTPUT ON to actually see it). T-SQL's free 'bare SELECT streams back to the caller' behavior has no PL/SQL equivalent — the procedure's signature itself needs a SYS_REFCURSOR OUT parameter, OPENed FOR the query, instead.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes what MySQL's STRICT_TRANS_TABLES mode actually does?
options: It makes MySQL reject invalid or missing data with a hard error, instead of silently coercing it with just a warning, for transactional storage engines like InnoDB
It disables all implicit type conversion between strings and numbers in every comparison
It enforces ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY automatically the moment it's enabled
It is MySQL's version of T-SQL's TRY/CATCH, converting runtime errors into a catchable exception block
It only affects MyISAM tables, since InnoDB is always strict by default regardless of sql_mode
It permanently alters the server's global sql_mode the instant any single session sets it
questions.explain: STRICT_TRANS_TABLES (and STRICT_ALL_TABLES for non-transactional engines too) changes how severely MySQL enforces data-validation rules: without it, something like inserting a too-long string truncates silently with a warning; with it, that same INSERT is a hard error, matching how SQL Server, Oracle, and PostgreSQL always behave. It's a per-session or per-server setting, and it is entirely independent of ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY, which is a separate sql_mode flag.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B sounds related because sql_mode does interact with implicit type conversion between strings and numbers, and strict mode reduces some of that leniency. But STRICT_TRANS_TABLES's actual job is turning invalid/missing-data warnings into hard errors for transactional engines — it isn't a blanket switch that disables all implicit type coercion everywhere. Conflating the two is exactly the kind of imprecise understanding this lesson warns against.

questions.prompt: A developer pastes this directly into the mysql command-line client without first running DELIMITER $$. What actually happens?
options: The client sends "CREATE PROCEDURE BadExample() BEGIN DECLARE x INT;" as soon as it hits the first semicolon, cutting the procedure definition off before it's complete — because the client, not the server, decides where a statement ends
The procedure is created successfully, because the server buffers the entire CREATE PROCEDURE statement regardless of which delimiter the client is using
MySQL automatically treats everything between BEGIN and END as one statement, DELIMITER or not
The client raises a clear "missing DELIMITER" error before sending anything to the server at all
questions.explain: The mysql command-line client (and tools that mimic it) uses ';' to decide when to send a statement to the server. A procedure body legitimately contains semicolons, so without DELIMITER changing that marker first, the client sends the statement the instant it hits the first internal semicolon — well before the END of the procedure. This is purely a client-tool limitation; the MySQL server itself has no concept of DELIMITER.

questions.prompt: After this ROLLBACK runs, what is the actual state of the data in the two tables?
options: The accounts row's balance change is undone, but the legacy_log row's message change is NOT undone, because MyISAM never participated in the transaction to begin with
Both changes are undone, since ROLLBACK always reverses every statement issued since START TRANSACTION, regardless of storage engine
Neither change is undone, because mixing storage engines inside one transaction block disables ROLLBACK entirely
An error is raised the moment the MyISAM UPDATE runs, because MyISAM tables can't appear inside a START TRANSACTION block at all
questions.explain: MyISAM has no transaction support at all, so it was never part of the transaction in the first place — ROLLBACK can only undo what InnoDB (or another transactional engine) actually tracked. The accounts UPDATE rolls back cleanly, but legacy_log's change silently stands, exactly the kind of production bug that comes from assuming every table behaves like InnoDB.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about MySQL's InnoDB and MyISAM storage engines, per Chapter 7.
options: InnoDB is MySQL's default storage engine since MySQL 5.5
MyISAM locks at the row level, the same granularity as InnoDB
A ROLLBACK against a MyISAM table silently does nothing, because MyISAM never participated in the transaction
MyISAM enforces foreign key constraints, just without transaction support
SHOW CREATE TABLE reveals a table's storage engine via its ENGINE=... clause
questions.explain: InnoDB has been MySQL's default since 5.5 and supports transactions, foreign keys, and row-level locking. MyISAM is the opposite on every count that matters here: it locks at the table level (not row level), has no foreign key enforcement at all, and has no transaction support — which is exactly why a ROLLBACK silently does nothing to a MyISAM table's changes. SHOW CREATE TABLE (and SHOW TABLE STATUS) both reveal a table's engine directly.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: once a MySQL stored procedure is created, you execute it with the keyword ________, not T-SQL's EXEC.
questions.explain: MySQL stored procedures are executed with CALL ProcedureName(), a different keyword from T-SQL's EXEC and from the informal EXEC convention sometimes used with PL/SQL.

questions.prompt: Match each MySQL term to what it actually is, per Chapter 7.
right: A client-tool directive that changes the end-of-statement marker, so a procedure body can contain ordinary semicolons
MySQL's pluggable mechanism for how a table actually stores and accesses its data, chosen per table
A system variable controlling how strictly the server validates data and enforces rules like NOT NULL
A mode enforcing the same GROUP BY rule T-SQL has always had; on by default since MySQL 5.7
questions.explain: sql_mode is the system variable controlling validation strictness. DELIMITER is purely a client-tool convention for writing multi-statement procedure bodies. ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY is the specific mode matching T-SQL's long-standing GROUP BY rule, default since MySQL 5.7. A storage engine is the pluggable per-table mechanism (InnoDB, MyISAM) controlling what features — transactions, foreign keys, locking granularity — a table actually supports.

questions.prompt: What is PostgreSQL's dollar-quoting ($$ ... $$) actually for?
options: Delimiting a string — such as a PL/pgSQL function body — without needing to escape single quotes used inside it
Marking a CTE as MATERIALIZED, so the planner treats it as an optimization fence
Declaring a column as a native ARRAY type instead of a scalar type
Casting a VARIANT or JSONB value to a specific scalar type before comparison
Replacing the WITH RECURSIVE keyword when starting a recursive CTE
Quoting an identifier so it preserves its exact case, the way double quotes do
questions.explain: Dollar-quoting delimits a code or string body — most commonly a PL/pgSQL function's body — so that single quotes used naturally inside it (like 'Hello, ' || name || '!') don't need escaping. Without it, every literal string inside the body would need doubled or escaped quotes. T-SQL has no equivalent, because a T-SQL procedure body is never itself a quoted string literal.
questions.distractorExplain: Option F is the tempting mix-up because both dollar-quoting and double-quoting involve a quoting mechanism. But they solve different problems: double-quoting an identifier ("Customers") preserves its exact case and makes it case-sensitive, a completely separate PostgreSQL behavior from dollar-quoting a function body's text. Dollar-quoting never touches identifier casing at all.

questions.prompt: What does this query actually return?
options: Exactly one row per customer_id — specifically each customer's most recent order — because DISTINCT ON keeps the first row per group according to the ORDER BY
Every row in orders, with duplicate customer_id values simply flagged rather than removed
One row per customer_id, but always the earliest order, regardless of how ORDER BY is written
An error, because DISTINCT ON requires every column in the SELECT list to also appear inside its parentheses
questions.explain: DISTINCT ON (customer_id) returns exactly one row per distinct customer_id — specifically whichever row sorts first under the given ORDER BY. Here ORDER BY customer_id, order_date DESC means the most recent order per customer wins. Getting a different row (like the earliest) would require reversing the ORDER BY, not changing DISTINCT ON itself.

questions.code:
-- payload = '{"user": {"name": "Pat", "age": 34}, "action": "login"}'
SELECT payload -> 'user' ->> 'name' FROM events;
questions.prompt: What does this expression return?
options: The plain text string Pat, because -> returns JSON for the intermediate step but ->> unwraps the final result to text
The JSON value {"name": "Pat", "age": 34}, because -> always wins over ->> when the two are chained
NULL, because -> and ->> cannot be chained together in the same expression
The quoted JSON string "Pat", including the surrounding quotation marks
questions.explain: payload -> 'user' returns the nested JSON object {"name": "Pat", "age": 34} (still JSON, quotes and nesting intact). Chaining ->> 'name' onto that result then unwraps the final step to plain text, returning Pat with no surrounding quotes. -> returns JSON at every step except the last one, where ->> is used instead.

questions.prompt: How is this function actually invoked once it exists?
options: SELECT get_customer_total(42); — called like any other expression-producing object, inside a SELECT, not with EXEC
EXEC get_customer_total(42); — the same EXEC syntax T-SQL stored procedures use
CALL get_customer_total(42); — PostgreSQL's dedicated keyword for running any PL/pgSQL object
RUN get_customer_total(42); — PostgreSQL's dedicated function-invocation keyword
questions.explain: PostgreSQL functions are called like any other expression-producing object, typically inside a SELECT — SELECT get_customer_total(42); — rather than with T-SQL's EXEC. (PostgreSQL's CALL keyword exists, but it's for CREATE PROCEDURE objects specifically, not ordinary CREATE FUNCTION objects like this one.)

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about PostgreSQL CTEs, per Chapter 8.
options: Before PostgreSQL 12, every CTE was always materialized — fully run and stored before being used in the outer query
On PostgreSQL 12+, a non-recursive CTE is inlined into the outer query by default unless explicitly marked MATERIALIZED
PostgreSQL allows a self-referencing CTE to recurse without any special keyword, exactly like T-SQL
WITH RECURSIVE is required in PostgreSQL for a recursive CTE, the same requirement MySQL has
Marking a CTE MATERIALIZED on PostgreSQL 12+ is meaningless, since the planner ignores the keyword entirely
questions.explain: Pre-12 PostgreSQL always treated a CTE as an optimization fence — fully materialized before the outer query used it. PostgreSQL 12 changed the default so non-recursive CTEs inline automatically, with MATERIALIZED available to force the old fenced behavior explicitly (so the keyword is far from meaningless). Unlike T-SQL and Oracle, PostgreSQL requires WITH RECURSIVE for a self-referencing CTE — the same requirement MySQL has.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: PostgreSQL has no ISNULL function at all — the standard function to use instead, which works identically across every dialect in this course, is ________().
questions.explain: PostgreSQL has no ISNULL function. COALESCE(expr1, expr2, ...) is the standard, multi-argument NULL-replacement function that works identically on T-SQL, Oracle, MySQL, and PostgreSQL alike.

questions.prompt: A T-SQL query needs a CTE wrapping ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...) plus a separate WHERE rn = 1 just to filter on the window function's result. What does Snowflake's QUALIFY clause let you do instead?
options: Filter directly on a window function's result in the same SELECT, without wrapping the query in a CTE or subquery at all
Automatically rank rows without needing to write ROW_NUMBER() or any window function
Replace GROUP BY entirely for any aggregate query
Convert a non-recursive CTE into a materialized one, the same role MATERIALIZED plays in PostgreSQL
questions.explain: QUALIFY filters directly on a window function's computed result in the same query that defines it — SELECT ... ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...) AS rn FROM orders QUALIFY rn = 1 — with no wrapping CTE or subquery needed. T-SQL has no equivalent shortcut; it genuinely requires the CTE-plus-WHERE pattern.

questions.prompt: A developer creates a Snowflake table with an unquoted name, Customers, then later runs SELECT * FROM "Customers";. What happens, and why?
options: It fails to find the table, because the unquoted CREATE folded the name to uppercase (CUSTOMERS) internally, but the quoted query preserves exact case and looks for a table literally named Customers
It works fine, because quoting an identifier in Snowflake is purely cosmetic and never changes case sensitivity
It works fine, because Snowflake folds quoted identifiers to uppercase too, the same as unquoted ones
It fails with a syntax error, because Snowflake doesn't support double-quoted identifiers at all
questions.explain: Snowflake identifiers are case-insensitive and folded to UPPERCASE internally when unquoted — the same family of behavior as Oracle. An unquoted CREATE TABLE Customers actually stores CUSTOMERS. Quoting an identifier preserves its exact case and makes it case-sensitive, so "Customers" looks for a table literally named Customers, which doesn't exist — it exists as CUSTOMERS.

questions.code:
-- payload = {"order": {"id": 501, "total": 129.99}}
SELECT payload:order.total::NUMBER AS order_total FROM events;
questions.prompt: Without the ::NUMBER cast at the end, what is payload:order.total before that cast is applied?
options: Still a VARIANT value, not yet a plain typed NUMBER — the colon/dot path reaches the field, but an explicit cast is needed to produce a properly typed scalar
Already a plain FLOAT, since Snowflake infers the scalar type automatically from JSON number literals
A text string containing "129.99", with quotation marks included
NULL, because dot notation can't reach a nested field without a preceding cast
questions.explain: A value reached through a VARIANT column's path (the : and chained dot/bracket notation) is still a VARIANT until explicitly cast with ::. Without the cast, comparisons and functions expecting a specific scalar type may not behave as expected — the :: operator is what actually produces a typed NUMBER, STRING, or other scalar.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Databricks SQL, per Chapter 9.
options: Databricks SQL quotes identifiers with backticks, the same convention MySQL uses
Databricks SQL tables are usually backed by Delta Lake, an open table format adding transactional guarantees over files in cloud storage
LATERAL VIEW explode() is syntactically identical to T-SQL's CROSS APPLY, just renamed
Databricks SQL's syntax traces back through Spark SQL to Hive SQL ancestry
Delta Lake is a separate product a team must explicitly opt into before writing any SQL against Databricks
questions.explain: Databricks SQL uses backtick identifier quoting, identical to MySQL's convention, and traces its syntax lineage through Spark SQL to Hive SQL. Its tables are usually backed by Delta Lake by default, not as a separate opt-in product. LATERAL VIEW explode() is conceptually similar to CROSS APPLY — both expand a per-row array/set into multiple output rows — but the actual syntax (a Spark-specific keyword combination vs. a JOIN-family keyword) is genuinely different, not just a rename.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about BigQuery and Redshift, per Chapter 9.
options: BigQuery's current Standard SQL dialect replaced an older, now-legacy SQL dialect it originally shipped with
Redshift is built on an older fork of PostgreSQL, making it the closest platform in this course to PostgreSQL syntax
BigQuery's fully-qualified table names are quoted with square brackets, the same convention T-SQL uses
Redshift's DISTKEY and SORTKEY are core SQL-language features every developer must master, not an administration concern
BigQuery has native ARRAY and STRUCT types, letting a single column hold a repeated value or a nested record directly
questions.explain: BigQuery's modern Standard SQL replaced its older legacy SQL dialect. Redshift is literally built on an older PostgreSQL fork, making it the closest match to PostgreSQL of any platform in this course. BigQuery quotes fully-qualified table names with backticks (`project.dataset.table`), not T-SQL-style square brackets, and has native ARRAY and STRUCT types. Redshift's DISTKEY/SORTKEY are physical-design and administration concerns, explicitly out of this course's language-focused scope.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Snowflake's string concatenation operator is ________, the same ANSI-standard operator PostgreSQL uses, replacing T-SQL's +.
questions.explain: Snowflake uses the ANSI-standard || operator for string concatenation, the same operator PostgreSQL uses. T-SQL's + does the same job but is MySQL's one real outlier, since || means logical OR there by default.

questions.prompt: A team is migrating a SQL Server application onto Azure SQL and wants a free compatibility assessment before running the actual migration. Which tool pairing does Chapter 10 identify for exactly this step?
options: Azure Database Migration Service (DMS), paired with the free Data Migration Assistant (DMA) for the compatibility assessment step
Oracle SQL Developer's Migration Workbench, since it accepts SQL Server as a source for any target platform
AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT), since it's the only tool that produces an assessment report at all
There is no tooling for this — compatibility assessment always has to be done by hand before an Azure migration
questions.explain: Azure Database Migration Service (DMS) migrates SQL Server workloads into Azure SQL Database or Azure SQL Managed Instance, and it's usually paired with the free Data Migration Assistant (DMA) specifically for the compatibility-assessment step, flagging blocking issues before the real migration runs.

questions.code:
-- Capstone query concatenates: p.FirstName + ' ' + p.LastName  (T-SQL)
-- Translating to MySQL, a developer writes:
p.first_name || ' ' || p.last_name
questions.prompt: Expecting this to concatenate the two names the same way the Oracle and PostgreSQL versions of the capstone query do, what actually happens when this runs on MySQL?
options: It's evaluated as a logical OR expression, not concatenation, unless PIPES_AS_CONCAT is explicitly enabled in sql_mode — CONCAT() is the safe, portable choice instead
It concatenates the two values exactly as intended, since || is ANSI-standard and MySQL supports it identically to PostgreSQL and Oracle
It raises a syntax error, because MySQL doesn't recognize the || token in any context
It silently returns NULL whenever || is used in place of CONCAT()
questions.explain: MySQL is the one genuine outlier among the capstone's three target platforms: unless the rarely-relied-upon PIPES_AS_CONCAT sql_mode flag is turned on, || means logical OR on MySQL, not string concatenation. CONCAT() is the only safe choice there, while Oracle and PostgreSQL both use || natively for this, exactly as T-SQL's + is replaced in each.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement from Chapter 10's translation-pitfalls checklist.
options: On Oracle, an empty string inserted into a VARCHAR2 column is actually stored as NULL, unlike on T-SQL, MySQL, and PostgreSQL
Quoted identifiers preserve exact case on Oracle and PostgreSQL, while T-SQL and MySQL don't fold case this way by default
Automated migration tools reliably translate procedural code like stored procedures and triggers, the same way they handle SELECT/JOIN/GROUP BY syntax
A date/time value that's valid on the source platform is always guaranteed to remain valid, and round the same way, on the target platform
MySQL's STRICT_TRANS_TABLES being part of the default sql_mode since 5.7 means every production MySQL database can be assumed to run in strict mode today
questions.explain: Oracle genuinely stores an empty VARCHAR2 as NULL at the storage level, and quoting preserves exact identifier case on Oracle/PostgreSQL where T-SQL/MySQL don't fold case the same way by default — both real checklist items. Automated tools consistently handle querying syntax well but need manual rework for procedural code, the opposite of option C. Date/time range and precision differences mean a value valid on the source platform is NOT guaranteed to remain valid or round the same way on the target. And plenty of production MySQL databases still run with a looser inherited sql_mode, so the current default can never simply be assumed.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: of the three sections every real migration guide covers — data type mappings, unsupported/different functions, and procedural code — the ________ section is consistently flagged as requiring the most manual rework.
questions.explain: Every real migration guide — Oracle's, AWS's, Microsoft's, Google's — eventually arrives at a procedural-code section (stored procedures, functions, triggers, packages), and every one says the same thing: automated tools translate basic query syntax well, but procedural objects almost always need a human to finish the job.

questions.prompt: Match each platform to its authoritative documentation source, per Chapter 10.
right: postgresql.org/docs
learn.microsoft.com
dev.mysql.com/doc/refman
docs.oracle.com
questions.explain: T-SQL's authoritative reference is learn.microsoft.com. Oracle's PL/SQL and Database SQL Language References live on docs.oracle.com. MySQL's official reference is the MySQL Reference Manual at dev.mysql.com/doc/refman. PostgreSQL's postgresql.org/docs is specifically called out as some of the best technical documentation in the open-source world.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of a real migration project, as Chapter 10 describes them, in the correct order.
items: Open the vendor's migration guide and start with its data type mapping table for source-to-target conversions
Check the guide's section listing unsupported or differently-behaving built-in functions
Run an automated migration tool, such as AWS SCT or Oracle's Migration Workbench, to convert the schema and generate an assessment report
Review the assessment report's action items for anything the tool could not convert automatically
Manually rework the procedural code the tool flagged, since stored procedures, functions, and triggers almost always need a human to finish the job
questions.explain: Every real migration guide is organized around the same three concerns in the same order of difficulty: data type mappings first, then unsupported/different functions, then procedural code. An automated tool applies those rules at scale and produces an assessment report of action items — but procedural code is consistently the section flagged as needing real manual rework afterward, since tools translate querying syntax well but can't safely guess procedural rewrites.
